scope_note: Entries marked 'abstract' were checked against the published abstract or publisher record only. Nobody on the team has read the full texts yet. Do that before quoting any figure to a jury.

studies.authors: Ge, L., Ng, A. H.-M., Li, X., Abidin, H. Z., Gumilar, I.
studies.title: Land subsidence characteristics of Bandung Basin as revealed by ENVISAT ASAR and ALOS PALSAR interferometry
studies.method: Time-series InSAR, compared against GPS surveys (2002-2010)
studies.reported: Displacement identified at Cimahi, Dayeuh Kolot, Rancaekek, Solokan Jeruk and Gedebage. Rates across the basin range from -240 to +40 mm/yr. Subsidence was steady in many areas, with acceleration in south Bandung. About 20-23 mm/yr of subsidence per 1 m/yr of groundwater-level decline.
studies.limitations: Causes are described as expected (groundwater extraction, soil consolidation under surface loading), with 'some correlations' to groundwater levels, not a demonstrated causal model.

studies.authors: Abidin, H. Z., Andreas, H., Gamal, M., Wirakusumah, A. D., Darmawan, D., Deguchi, T., Maruyama, Y.
studies.title: Land subsidence characteristics of the Bandung Basin, Indonesia, as estimated from GPS and InSAR
studies.method: Five repeated GPS surveys plus InSAR
studies.reported: A few locations subsided by about 70 cm over the five years, at roughly 1-2 cm/month. InSAR showed a similar rate and detected significant subsidence in the textile-industry area.
studies.limitations: Statistical testing found no strong correlation between GPS-derived subsidence and registered groundwater extraction for February 2000 - July 2002.

studies.authors: Du, Z., Ge, L., Ng, A. H.-M., Zhu, Q., Yang, X., Li, L.
studies.title: Correlating the subsidence pattern and land use in Bandung, Indonesia with both Sentinel-1/2 and ALOS-2 satellite images
studies.venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation 67, 54-68
studies.method: Time-series InSAR, the two sensors cross-validated
studies.reported: Six '10-cm subsidence zones' (A-F). Vertical motion dominates the line-of-sight signal. Industrial groundwater use is not always the dominant cause: subsidence reflects residential, industrial and agricultural activity combined.
studies.limitations: The dominant factor inside each zone could not be identified for lack of statistics such as groundwater use per square kilometre.

studies.authors: Rygus, M., Bianchi, M., Novellino, A., Hussain, E., Taufiq, A., Rusli, S. R., Sarah, D., Meisina, C.
studies.title: Permanent aquifer storage loss from long-term groundwater withdrawal: a case study of subsidence in Bandung (Indonesia)
studies.satellites: InSAR-derived displacement used to calibrate the model
studies.method: 3-D hydro-geomechanical groundwater model calibrated against InSAR
studies.reported: Peak simulated subsidence 16.4 cm/yr, maximum cumulative 6.9 m, permanent aquifer storage loss 7.2 km3. With continued industrial extraction: up to 5.6 m more subsidence by 2050.
studies.limitations: These are model results, not direct measurements. Historical pumping data are scarce and were estimated through the calibration.

studies.authors: Chaussard, E., Amelung, F., Abidin, H., Hong, S.-H.
studies.title: Sinking cities in Indonesia: ALOS PALSAR detects rapid subsidence due to groundwater and gas extraction
studies.method: Time-series InSAR from over 900 ALOS images on 33 ascending tracks
studies.reported: Significant subsidence in nine areas including Bandung, at rates up to 22 cm/yr across all sites. For Bandung: maximum vertical rate 22.5 cm/yr and average 7.2 cm/yr (Table 2); the paper also cites GPS surveys (2000-2010) showing 8-23 cm/yr.
studies.limitations: Regional survey of many cities at once; later work argues local studies need finer processing and ground data.
